scope: Complete four-page main and six figures plus the 28-entry bibliography; any SI and cited full sources remain unreviewed.

bibliographic_scope.title: Optical Properties of Colloidal PbSe Nanocrystals
bibliographic_scope.authors: Hui Du; Chialing Chen; Rishikesh Krishnan; Todd D. Krauss; Jeffrey M. Harbold; Frank W. Wise; Malcolm G. Thomas; John Silcox

preparation_scope.method_reference: Modified Murray et al. method, reference 19; cited full method unreviewed. Only charges/conditions actually given here are used.
preparation_scope.supplier: TOP from Fluka; all other reagents from Aldrich. Purities unreported.

injection.injected_volume: Not reported; not equated to capacity

growth.relationship: Higher injection/growth temperatures yield larger dots; exact assignments absent

workup.repetition: Source says procedure repeated twice; total normalized cycles not assigned
workup.size_selection: Not necessary under favorable growth conditions; no compulsory size-selective precipitation procedure supplied

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and analytical preparation

XRD.sample_preparation: Evaporate several drops of nanocrystal sample on special low-background sample-holder plate
XRD.result: Rock-salt PbSe with the lattice constant of bulk PbSe; numeric cell parameter not stated
XRD.impurity: Asterisked peaks in Figure 1 assigned to trace unreacted lead oleate
XRD.size: XRD width estimates said to agree with electron microscopy, without numeric per-pattern estimates

STEM.instrument: Vacuum Generators HB501UX with high-resolution pole piece
STEM.sample: Approximately 20 µL drop in hexane or tetrachloroethylene on holey-carbon film on a 300-mesh copper grid
STEM.signals: Bright-field and annular dark-field simultaneously acquired; software reference 20
STEM.Figure2_left: Low-resolution ensemble in locally ordered close-packed array; full image scale 320 nm
STEM.Figure2_right: Approximately 7 nm particle with hexagonal array of Pb columns; full image scale 12.8 nm; authors infer a defect-free single crystal from this image
STEM.interpretation_limit: No quantitative defect statistics, shape distribution or 3D atom positions

structural_characterization.size_series: Continuous 3–8 nm preparation range; specific 3,approximately 7 and approximately 8 nm contexts recorded. Unlabelled Figure 3 curves are not turned into invented discrete recipes.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, XRD/STEM methods and Figures 1–2

optical_methods.fluorescence: Acton Research modular system; emission collected at right angle to excitation, InGaAs photodiode detection
optical_methods.optical_density: Less than 0.1 at lowest exciton for all fluorescence samples

QY_reference.source: Reference 21; calibrator concentration and preparation not supplied

optical_methods.decay: PicoQuant FluoTime 200 time-correlated single-photon counting; 880 nm pulsed diode excitation; cooled Ge avalanche photodiode; recorded at peak emission wavelength

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2, 4, Optical methods and Figure 6 caption

optical_results.abstract_QY: As high as 80%; rounded abstract wording, body maximum 81% retained

absorption.size_variation_basis: Authors estimate from optical absorption, said consistent with STEM; definition/uncertainty unreported
absorption.Figure3: Curves cover 3–8 nm; no complete numerical size-to-curve crosswalk

Figure4.bars: Calculated allowed one-photon transitions using Kang formalism (reference 15)
Figure4.conclusion: Second absorption feature not decisively assigned; first/third match model, systematic discrepancy for diameters below 5 nm

luminescence.below1400nm_features: Authors do not believe these small features intrinsic
luminescence.inorganic_shell_passivation: Not used; no extra shell recipe

decays.list_scope: Three Figure 5 optical samples; sizes and physical batches not resolved. Values retained without assigning 330/360 ns to named 7/8 nm products. Uncertainty convention not supplied.
decays.trend: Increasing decay time with increasing size, as source reports

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1–4, Abstract, optical results and Figures 3–6

theory_and_context.scope: Background/reference scales and literal source ratio, not recomputed particle descriptors.
theory_and_context.source_reference28_note: Later dielectric-screening calculation reportedly explains approximately 0.1 µs decays; this is the authors’ note and the cited article is not newly reviewed here.

radiative_lifetime_estimates.dielectric_screening_increase: As much as two orders of magnitude if bulk PbSe dielectric constants are assumed
radiative_lifetime_estimates.qualification: The source questions whether bulk material parameters apply to the nanocrystals. These are theoretical estimates, not measured product values or new specimens.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 4, radiative-lifetime discussion preceding reference 28

source_interpretation.topic: Why use colloidal PbSe quantum dots
source_interpretation.text: The authors motivate PbSe by its strong confinement and infrared transitions. They cite electron, hole and exciton Bohr radii of 23, 23 and 46 nm and describe a 3–8 nm colloidal size range. These are background/model scales, not particle-coordinate measurements. The source’s stated R/aB range is retained without recalculation or redefinition.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction and reported confinement range

source_interpretation.topic: Temperature controls a series, not a supplied exact sample schedule
source_interpretation.text: The paper varies injection and growth temperature within 80–150 °C and holds growth for 5–10 min. Higher temperatures produce larger dots, but it does not provide an exact temperature/time for each displayed size. The resulting record preserves that relationship without assigning endpoint temperatures to particular specimens.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and size-control paragraphs

source_interpretation.text: Lead acetate and oleic acid are heated in phenyl ether, cooled, mixed with the reported TOPSe stock, then injected into hot phenyl ether. The paper gives syringe capacity but no measured precursor volume. Repeated precipitation and centrifugation remove excess reagents; size-selective precipitation is stated to be unnecessary under favorable conditions, not mandatory as a separate unreported step.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and analytical sample preparation

source_interpretation.text: XRD is assigned to rock-salt PbSe and explicitly shows trace lead-oleate precursor peaks. STEM shows a close-packed ensemble and an approximately 7 nm lattice-resolved particle. The authors interpret its Pb-column image as a single crystal without internal defects, but no batch-wide defect fraction, shape distribution or atomic coordinate refinement is supplied.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 1–2 and structure discussion

source_interpretation.topic: Optical transitions are not all uniquely assigned
source_interpretation.text: The authors compare the approximately 8 nm absorption spectrum with Kang’s model. First and third transitions agree, while the second feature is not accounted for by the allowed-transition calculation. Parity-forbidden transitions and band anisotropy are discussed as alternatives; the article favors the former but states that no decisive assignment is made. Model arrows and bars are not additional measured materials.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transition interpretation; references 15 and 22

source_interpretation.topic: High quantum yield does not prove a measured surface structure
source_interpretation.text: The main reports room-temperature quantum yields of 12–81% without an inorganic semiconductor shell. Variation in surface reconstruction at reaction termination is suggested as an explanation, with comparison to earlier CdSe work. Actual surface reconstruction, ligand coverage and a per-size QY table are not measured.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 5 and quantum-yield discussion; reference 27

source_interpretation.topic: Long-lived emission and the later theoretical note
source_interpretation.text: The 3 nm decay shown in Figure 6 has a 250 ns fitted time constant. The authors estimate an unscreened lowest-exciton transition-dipole radiative lifetime on the order of nanoseconds. They estimate that dielectric screening could increase it by as much as two orders of magnitude if bulk PbSe dielectric constants are assumed, while explicitly questioning whether bulk parameters apply to these nanocrystals. These are theoretical estimates, not additional measured lifetimes. Reference 28 adds a note that later calculations account for approximately 0.1 µs decay times; that cited full paper is not reviewed in this contribution, so the note remains source-attributed rather than independently confirmed.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figure 6, decay discussion and reference 28

source_interpretation.topic: Stokes shifts and application outlook remain qualified
source_interpretation.text: Ensemble Stokes shifts of 40–90 meV are reported, but excitation well above the lowest exciton prevents direct identification with an intrinsic single-particle spectrum. Vibronic/non-Franck–Condon effects are proposed. Optoelectronics and fluorescence microscopy are motivations; no device performance or biological test is reported here.

evidence.locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3–4, Abstract, Stokes-shift discussion and outlook; reference 23
